name: Nail buffer block

lead: A nail buffer block is a small foam or rubber-like block with sides of different grit. It smooths ridges and polishes the nail surface so nails look even and glossy without polish.
The payoff is neat, healthy-looking hands. Buffing is a standard manicure step, though no clinical studies of buffer blocks are cited here.

paras: Buffers are used from coarse to fine sides: a medium grit smooths ridges, a finer one gives a matte finish, and the finest produces shine. Buffing is also used to roughen nails slightly before gel or polish.
Pressing hard can create heat and pain and may lead to infection, and over-buffing wears down the nail plate; only about 5% of its thickness should be removed according to the source.

angle.text: Buffing evens out the nail surface and creates a natural shine, making hands look groomed without polish.

lead: A nail buffer block polishes the nail surface using progressively finer grits so nails look smoother, more even and shinier.[1] Modern buffers resemble large rubber erasers with a different coarseness on each side.[1]

In use, a medium grit smooths ridges and irregularities, a fine grit gives a matte finish, and the finest grit gives a glossy shine.[1] Emery boards are meant for shaping the nail edge, not for buffing.[1] Buffing also helps polish and artificial nails adhere.[1]

paras: Traditional buffing used buffing cream and chamois leather; modern blocks have multiple grit sides.[1] Buffing paste can fill ridges.[1]

Pressing too hard can cause heat and pain and may lead to infection. Over-buffing, especially over long periods, can wear down the nail plate; the source says only about 5% of the plate's thickness should be removed.[1]
